extracted.intended_audience: readers and reviewers of poetry; general literary readers and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to judge and appreciate metrical/lyric poetry: what to look for (matter, feeling, aim) and how to form fair literary judgments rather than relying on prejudice or mere formal features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by personal feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: That in judging these Poems he would decide by his own feelings genuinely, and not by reflection upon what will probably be the judgment of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author requests readers to abide independently by their own feelings; warns against the common critical habit of tempering one’s taste by imagining how others (or certain classes of people) will judge. This external-concern mode of criticism is described as 'destructive of all sound unadulterated judgment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the matter (sense/content) rather than metre or diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Not from the metre, not from the language, not from the order of the words; but the matter expressed ... is contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a comparison of two stanzas with identical words/order but different effect, the page argues that formal features (metre, language, word order) are not decisive; the subject-matter and what it actually expresses determine poetic value. The criterion is whether the matter is interesting and capable of exciting thought and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivial/simple verses 'want sense' (failure of poetic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper method of treating trivial and simple verses ... is to say this ... wants sense; it is neither interesting in itself, nor can lead to any thing interesting; the images neither originate in that sane state of feeling which arises out of thought, nor can excite thought or feeling in the Reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When verses are trivial, call the defect 'want of sense' rather than merely arguing about whether they belong to a certain species of poetry. Focus criticism on the lack of originating feeling and inability to provoke thought — these are substantive failures, not merely stylistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide genus before species (avoid premature classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Why trouble yourself about the species till you have previously decided upon the genus? Why take pains to prove that an Ape is not a Newton when it is self-evident that he is not a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not waste effort disputing fine-grained categories or labels before determining whether the work attains the broader qualities that make it poetry (or good poetry). Establish the overall kind/quality first, then discuss taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give authors presumption from works that impress
rubrics_metrics.description: If an Author by any single composition has impressed us with respect for his talents, it is useful to consider this as affording a presumption, that, on other occasions where we have been displeased, he nevertheless may not have written ill or absurdly;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a successful composition as a reason to re-examine or temper negative judgments of an author's other works; this is both an act of justice and a way to improve one's own taste by avoiding rash rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an accurate taste by study of the best models
rubrics_metrics.description: An accurate taste in Poetry and in all the other arts ... is an acquired talent, which can only be produced by thought and a long continued intercourse with the best models of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good critical judgment is acquired: spend time with exemplary works and reflect. Readers inexperienced in poetry are warned that their judgments may be erroneous and that patience and exposure to high models are needed to form sound taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge both the poet's aim and the poet's success
rubrics_metrics.description: He will determine how far I have attained this object; and, what is a much more important question, whether it be worth attaining;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should ask (a) what the poet set out to do and whether they achieved it, and (b) whether that aim itself is valuable. Both questions bear on the work’s claim to public approbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to different kinds of poetic pleasure (and willing to relinquish old preferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Reader is himself conscious of the pleasure which he has received from such composition ... we not only wish to be pleased, but to be pleased in that particular way in which we have been accustomed to be pleased ... in order entirely to enjoy the Poetry which I am recommending, it would be necessary to give up much of what is ordinarily enjoyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should recognize that new modes of poetry may offer purer or different pleasures; fully appreciating them may require letting go of habitual tastes. Expect resistance but consider whether new forms provide lasting and higher enjoyment.
